verse.text: What was from the beginning, what we have heard, what we have seen with our eyes, what we looked upon and our hands touched, concerning the Logos of life—
verse.note: The phrase can refer to the absolute beginning, echoing the opening of John's Gospel, or to the beginning of the Christian message in the ministry of Jesus. Elsewhere in this letter it usually means the start of the readers' own hearing of the message (2:7, 2:24). The translation leaves both open, as the Greek does.

Nearly all translations have 'the Word of life'. This translation uses 'Logos' where the term echoes the title of John 1:1, because 'the Word' is now commonly heard as meaning the Bible. The sense here is disputed. The opening pronoun is neuter ('what', not 'who'), and many scholars take the phrase to mean the life-giving message about Jesus and not the personal Word himself; the wording may deliberately hold the two together.

verse.text: and the life was revealed, and we have seen it and testify to it and declare to you the eternal life that was with the Father and was revealed to us—
verse.note: The Greek adjective is formed from the word for 'age'. In Jewish usage 'eternal life' is the life of the age to come, so the phrase describes a kind of life as well as its unending length. Here that life is said to have already appeared in a person who could be seen and touched.

verse.text: what we have seen and heard we declare to you also, so that you too may have fellowship with us. And our fellowship is with the Father and with his Son Jesus Christ.
verse.note: The Greek word means having something in common: partnership, a shared stake, joint participation. It was used of business partnerships and of marriage as well as of friendship. It is a stronger term than the friendly sociability that 'fellowship' can suggest in modern English.

verse.text: And we are writing these things so that our joy may be complete.

note.term: we are writing these things so that our joy
note.traditional: these things write we unto you, that your joy may be full

verse.note: Many manuscripts read 'we write to you' and 'your joy', and the King James tradition follows them. The earliest witnesses favour 'we' and 'our', and copyists were more likely to change the unexpected 'our joy' to 'your joy' than the reverse. In Greek the two readings differ by a single letter in each word.

verse.text: And this is the message that we have heard from him and announce to you: that God is light, and in him there is no darkness at all.
If we say that we have fellowship with him and yet walk in the darkness, we lie and do not do the truth.
verse.note: 'Doing the truth' is a Semitic turn of phrase, found also at John 3:21, in which truth is something acted on and not only believed or spoken. The translation keeps the idiom; the sense is 'our conduct is not true'.

verse.text: But if we walk in the light as he himself is in the light, we have fellowship with one another, and the blood of Jesus his Son cleanses us from all sin.
If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us.
If we confess our sins, he is faithful and righteous to forgive us our sins and cleanse us from all unrighteousness.
verse.note: Most English versions read 'faithful and just'. Greek has a single word-family where English has two (righteous/just, righteousness/justice), and 'unrighteousness' at the end of the verse is the negative of the same word. 'Righteous' keeps that link audible: the one who is in the right cleanses from all that is not right.

verse.text: If we say that we have not sinned, we make him a liar, and his word is not in us.
verse.note: The Greek noun is the one rendered 'Logos' in verse 1, but here it has its ordinary sense of God's spoken message, parallel to 'the truth is not in us' in verse 8. It is therefore translated 'word', as in all standard versions.

verse.text: My little children, I am writing these things to you so that you may not sin. But if anyone does sin, we have an Advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ, the righteous one,
verse.note: The word was used of someone who speaks up on another's behalf, as a supporter might before a judge. In John's Gospel the same word is used of the Spirit, where older English versions have 'Comforter'. Here it is Jesus who speaks for believers before the Father, and English versions have long used 'advocate' in this verse.

verse.text: and he himself is the atoning sacrifice for our sins, and not for ours only but also for the whole world.
verse.note: The word belongs to the Septuagint's vocabulary of atonement and the forgiveness it brings. 'Propitiation' (turning away wrath) and 'expiation' (removing sin) each take one side of a long-running dispute. 'Atoning sacrifice', used by several modern versions, leaves that question open. The noun occurs in the New Testament only here and at 4:10.

verse.text: And by this we know that we have come to know him: if we keep his commandments.
The one who says, “I have come to know him,” and does not keep his commandments is a liar, and the truth is not in that person;
but whoever keeps his word, in that person the love of God has truly been made complete. By this we know that we are in him:
verse.note: The Greek can mean a person's love for God, God's love for that person, or the kind of love that comes from God. The translation keeps the open phrase. The same question arises with 'the love of the Father' in verse 15, where love for the Father is the more likely sense because it is set against loving the world.

verse.text: the one who says he remains in him ought himself to walk just as he walked.
verse.note: The traditional 'abide' has dropped out of ordinary English. The Greek verb is the everyday word for staying or remaining, and the letter uses it repeatedly, of people remaining in God, of God's word remaining in them, and in verse 19 of those who did not remain with the community. One English verb is used throughout so that the repetition can be heard.
The Greek here switches to a distinct pronoun, literally 'that one', which in this letter regularly points to Jesus. 'Walk' is the common Jewish idiom for how a person conducts their life.

verse.text: Beloved, I am not writing you a new commandment, but an old commandment that you have had from the beginning. The old commandment is the word that you heard.
On the other hand, I am writing you a new commandment, which is true in him and in you, because the darkness is passing away and the true light is already shining.
The one who says he is in the light and hates his brother is in the darkness even now.
verse.note: In this letter 'brother' means a fellow member of the believing community, whether a man or a woman, not a sibling. Some modern versions render 'brother or sister' or 'fellow believer'. The masculine singular here and in the following verses is generic.

verse.text: The one who loves his brother remains in the light, and in him there is no cause for stumbling;

note.term: in him there is no cause for stumbling
note.traditional: there is none occasion of stumbling in him

verse.note: The word refers to a trap or obstacle that makes someone fall. The Greek may mean that there is nothing in such a person to trip him up, or nothing in him that makes others fall. The pronoun could also be read as 'in it', meaning that in the light there is nothing to stumble over.

verse.text: but the one who hates his brother is in the darkness and walks in the darkness, and does not know where he is going, because the darkness has blinded his eyes.
I am writing to you, little children, because your sins have been forgiven on account of his name.
verse.note: Throughout verses 12 to 14 the Greek conjunction can mean either 'because' (giving the reason for writing) or 'that' (giving the content of what is written, as in 'I write to tell you that your sins have been forgiven'). Most translations choose 'because', but the other reading is well supported.

verse.text: I am writing to you, fathers, because you have come to know the one who is from the beginning. I am writing to you, young men, because you have overcome the evil one.

I have written to you, children, because you have come to know the Father. I have written to you, fathers, because you have come to know the one who is from the beginning. I have written to you, young men, because you are strong, and the word of God remains in you, and you have overcome the evil one.
verse.note: The verb shifts from the present tense in verses 12 and 13 to a past tense here. Most interpreters take this as a stylistic variation that still refers to the present letter, since Greek letter-writers often used a past tense from the reader's point of view. Some think an earlier writing is meant. Some editions and translations number the first sentence of this verse as the end of verse 13.

verse.text: Do not love the world or the things in the world. If anyone loves the world, the love of the Father is not in him;
because everything in the world, the desire of the flesh and the desire of the eyes and the boastful pride in possessions, is not from the Father but is from the world.
verse.note: The first noun means showy boasting or pretension. The word for 'life' here is not the one used for eternal life but the one for livelihood or material means, as at 3:17. The traditional 'pride of life' suggests pride in being alive or in life generally, whereas the Greek points to showing off what one has. Several modern versions render it similarly ('pride in riches', 'pride in one's possessions').

verse.text: And the world is passing away, and its desire with it, but the one who does the will of God remains forever.
Children, it is the last hour, and just as you heard that antichrist is coming, so now many antichrists have appeared. From this we know that it is the last hour.
verse.note: The word occurs in the New Testament only in 1 and 2 John. Its prefix can mean both 'against' and 'in place of', so it names an opponent of Christ or a rival claimant to his place. The author assumes that his readers already expect such a figure and applies the term to those who have left the community and deny that Jesus is the Christ (verses 19 and 22).

verse.text: They went out from us, but they were not of us; for if they had been of us, they would have remained with us. But they went out so that it might be revealed that none of them is of us.
And you have an anointing from the Holy One, and you all know.
verse.note: The Greek word is closely related to 'Christ' (the anointed one) and so also to 'antichrist': the readers have an anointing where the opponents are anti-anointed. Most interpreters take the anointing to be the Holy Spirit given to believers. Some take it as the teaching they received at the beginning, or both together.

Many later manuscripts read 'you know all things', which the King James Version follows. The reading translated here, 'you all know', is found in important early manuscripts and is preferred by most modern editors. It fits the argument that knowledge belongs to every member of the community and not to a select few.

verse.text: I have not written to you because you do not know the truth, but because you know it, and because no lie is from the truth.
Who is the liar, if not the one who denies that Jesus is the Christ? This is the antichrist: the one who denies the Father and the Son.
Everyone who denies the Son does not have the Father either; the one who acknowledges the Son has the Father also.
As for you, let what you heard from the beginning remain in you. If what you heard from the beginning remains in you, you also will remain in the Son and in the Father.
And this is the promise that he himself promised us: eternal life.
I have written these things to you about those who are trying to lead you astray.

As for you, the anointing that you received from him remains in you, and you have no need for anyone to teach you. But as his anointing teaches you about all things, and is true and is no lie, and just as it has taught you, remain in him.
verse.note: The Greek verb form can be either a command ('remain') or a statement ('you remain'), and the pronoun can mean 'in him' or 'in it', that is, in the anointing or its teaching. The command reading is chosen because the next verse repeats the same words as an unmistakable command. The long sentence leading up to it can also be punctuated in more than one way.

verse.text: And now, little children, remain in him, so that when he is revealed we may have confidence and not shrink from him in shame at his coming.
verse.note: The word means arrival and the presence that follows. It was the regular term for the state visit of a king or high official, an occasion for which a city prepared itself. This is its only occurrence in the letters and Gospel of John.

verse.text: If you know that he is righteous, you know that everyone who practices righteousness has been born of him.
See what kind of love the Father has given us: that we should be called children of God—and so we are. This is why the world does not know us: it did not know him.
Beloved, now we are children of God, and what we will be has not yet been revealed. We know that when he is revealed we will be like him, because we will see him as he is.
verse.note: The Greek verb has no expressed subject, so it can also be read 'when it is revealed', that is, when what we will be is made known. The rendering follows 2:28, where the same expression clearly refers to Christ's coming, and most translations do likewise. The word translated 'when' does not imply doubt about the event.

verse.text: And everyone who has this hope set on him purifies themselves, just as he is pure.
verse.note: Here and in verses 5, 7 and 16 the Greek says 'that one', a pronoun this letter uses to point to Jesus without naming him. English 'he' cannot show the distinction, but in each case the reference is to Christ.

verse.text: Everyone who practices sin also practices lawlessness, and sin is lawlessness.
And you know that he was revealed in order to take away sins, and in him there is no sin.
No one who remains in him sins; no one who sins has seen him or known him.

note.traditional: sinneth not / does not keep on sinning

verse.note: The Greek is a plain present tense, as in verse 9 ('cannot sin'). Many modern translations render 'keeps on sinning' or 'makes a practice of sinning', taking the tense to describe a habit, which eases the tension with 1:8–2:1, where believers are said to sin. Whether the tense alone can carry that weight is disputed, so the text leaves the statement as stark as the Greek. 'Practices sin' in verses 4, 8 and 9 renders a different expression, literally 'does sin', the counterpart of 'does righteousness'.

The traditional 'abide' is now archaic. The Greek is the ordinary word for staying or remaining somewhere, and the letter uses it repeatedly (verses 6, 9, 14, 15, 17, 24). 'Remains' is used throughout so that the repetition is visible.

verse.text: Little children, let no one deceive you. Whoever practices righteousness is righteous, just as he is righteous.
verse.note: Greek has a single word-family where English has two: 'righteous' and 'just', 'righteousness' and 'justice'. In this chapter the sense is doing what is right, and 'righteous' in verses 7 and 12 is the matching adjective.

verse.text: Whoever practices sin is of the devil, because the devil has been sinning from the beginning. The Son of God was revealed for this: to destroy the works of the devil.
No one who has been born of God practices sin, because God's seed remains in them; and they cannot sin, because they have been born of God.
verse.note: The Greek is literally 'his seed remains in him'. Most interpreters take it as God's seed remaining in the believer, an image of divine life implanted at birth from God, variously identified with the Spirit or the word. Since 'seed' can also mean offspring, a minority read 'God's offspring remain in him', that is, in God.

verse.text: By this the children of God and the children of the devil are revealed: anyone who does not practice righteousness is not of God, nor is anyone who does not love their brother or sister.
verse.note: The Greek word is grammatically masculine but was the ordinary way of referring to fellow members of the community, women included. It is rendered 'brother or sister', and in the plural 'brothers and sisters', as several recent translations do. In verse 12 it is Cain's literal brother Abel, and the Greek reader would hear the same word throughout.

verse.text: For this is the message you heard from the beginning: that we should love one another,
not like Cain, who was of the evil one and slaughtered his brother. And why did he slaughter him? Because his own works were evil and his brother's were righteous.
verse.note: The verb is not the usual word for killing. It is used of butchering animals and of violent, bloody killing; outside this verse the New Testament uses it only in Revelation. Most translations have 'murdered' or 'killed'; 'slaughtered' keeps the brutality of the word.

verse.text: Do not be surprised, brothers and sisters, if the world hates you.
We know that we have crossed over from death into life, because we love the brothers and sisters. Whoever does not love remains in death.
Everyone who hates their brother or sister is a murderer, and you know that no murderer has eternal life remaining in them.
verse.note: In Jewish usage 'eternal life' is the life of the age to come, so the phrase speaks of a kind of life as well as its unending length. In this letter that life is something believers already have, as verse 14 says.

verse.text: By this we have come to know love: he laid down his life for us. And we ought to lay down our lives for the brothers and sisters.
But whoever has the world's goods and sees their brother or sister in need, yet closes off compassion toward them—how does the love of God remain in such a person?

note.traditional: shutteth up his bowels of compassion / closes his heart

verse.note: The Greek word means the inward parts, regarded as the seat of pity and tender feeling. Modern translations often say 'heart', but a different Greek word for 'heart' follows in verses 19–21, so 'compassion' is used here to keep the two apart.

verse.text: Little children, let us not love with word or with tongue, but in deed and truth.
By this we will know that we are of the truth, and in his presence we will set our hearts at rest
verse.note: The grammar of verses 19–20 is among the most difficult in the letter. The verb normally means 'persuade', and the Greek of verse 20 has two connecting words that can each be read as 'that', 'because' or, in the first case, 'whenever'. The rendering follows the common view that God's greater knowledge is a comfort to a self-accusing conscience. Others read 'we will convince our hearts that God is greater', and a few take God's greatness as a warning, not a reassurance.

verse.text: whenever our hearts condemn us; for God is greater than our hearts, and he knows everything.
Beloved, if our hearts do not condemn us, we have confidence before God,
and whatever we ask we receive from him, because we keep his commandments and do what is pleasing in his sight.
And this is his commandment: that we believe in the name of his Son Jesus Christ and love one another, just as he commanded us.
And whoever keeps his commandments remains in him, and he in that person. And by this we know that he remains in us: by the Spirit he gave us.
Beloved, do not believe every spirit, but test the spirits to see whether they are from God, because many false prophets have gone out into the world.
By this you know the Spirit of God: every spirit that acknowledges Jesus Christ as having come in the flesh is from God,
verse.note: The Greek verb means to declare openly or agree publicly to something. ‘Confess’ is the traditional rendering, but in modern English it mainly suggests admitting wrongdoing, which is not the sense here. Several modern translations also use ‘acknowledge’.

note.term: Jesus Christ as having come in the flesh
note.traditional: that Jesus Christ is come in the flesh

verse.note: The Greek can be construed in three ways: acknowledging ‘Jesus Christ, come in the flesh’ (the person so described), acknowledging ‘that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh’ (the fact), or acknowledging ‘Jesus as the Christ come in the flesh’. The rendering here follows the first, which stays closest to the grammar. All three are aimed at teachers who denied that the Son of God was a real human being. The verb ‘you know’ could also be read as a command, ‘know’.

verse.text: and every spirit that does not acknowledge Jesus is not from God. This is the spirit of the antichrist, which you have heard is coming, and now it is already in the world.

note.traditional: confesseth not that Jesus Christ is come in the flesh

verse.note: Many later manuscripts expand this to match verse 2 (‘does not confess that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh’), which is the reading behind the King James Version. A few ancient witnesses, mostly Latin and patristic, read ‘annuls Jesus’ or ‘separates Jesus’ instead of ‘does not acknowledge’. Most editors judge the short reading translated here to be original.

verse.text: You are from God, little children, and you have overcome them, because the one who is in you is greater than the one who is in the world.
They are from the world; that is why they speak from the world, and the world listens to them.
We are from God. Whoever knows God listens to us; whoever is not from God does not listen to us. From this we know the Spirit of truth and the spirit of error.

note.term: the Spirit of truth and the spirit of error
note.traditional: the spirit of truth, and the spirit of error

verse.note: Greek manuscripts do not distinguish capital from lower-case letters, so whether ‘Spirit of truth’ means the Holy Spirit (as in John 14:17) or more generally a spirit that inspires true teaching is an interpreter's decision. The capital here follows verse 2, where the Spirit of God is the standard for the test. The word rendered ‘error’ can also mean ‘deception’, a going or leading astray.

verse.text: Beloved, let us love one another, because love is from God, and everyone who loves has been born of God and knows God.
Whoever does not love has not come to know God, because God is love.
In this the love of God was revealed among us: that God has sent his one and only Son into the world so that we might live through him.
verse.note: The word describes someone who is the only one of a kind, and was the ordinary term for an only child. Its second element is related to ‘kind’ rather than ‘beget’, so ‘one and only’ is now the usual rendering. A minority of scholars have recently defended ‘only begotten’.

The Greek phrase is literally ‘in us’, and can mean ‘among us’, ‘within us’ or ‘in our case’. The same phrase occurs in verse 16, where it is rendered ‘for us’ because the love is something God ‘has’. In verse 12 it is rendered ‘in us’ because it follows the verb ‘remains’.

verse.text: In this is love: not that we have loved God, but that he loved us and sent his Son as the atoning sacrifice for our sins.
verse.note: In the Greek Old Testament this word and its relatives are used for atonement and for offerings that deal with sin. The traditional ‘propitiation’ stresses the turning away of divine wrath, while others prefer ‘expiation’, the removal of sin. The dispute is long-running, and ‘atoning sacrifice’ leaves room for both senses in plain English.

verse.text: Beloved, if God loved us in this way, we also ought to love one another.
No one has ever seen God. If we love one another, God remains in us, and his love has been perfected in us.
verse.note: This is the everyday Greek verb for staying or remaining somewhere, and a favourite of this author for a lasting relationship with God. ‘Abide’ is the traditional rendering but is now archaic. ‘Remain’ is used for it throughout the chapter so that the repetition stays visible.

note.term: his love has been perfected in us
note.traditional: his love is perfected in us

verse.note: ‘His love’ may mean God's love for us, our love for God, or the kind of love that is God's; most interpreters take it as God's love reaching its intended goal when believers love one another. ‘Perfected’ here means brought to its full end or completion. It does not mean made flawless.

verse.text: By this we know that we remain in him and he in us: that he has given us of his Spirit.
And we have seen and testify that the Father has sent the Son as Savior of the world.
Whoever acknowledges that Jesus is the Son of God, God remains in them and they in God.
And we have come to know and have believed the love that God has for us. God is love, and whoever remains in love remains in God, and God remains in them.
In this love has been perfected with us, so that we may have confidence on the day of judgment: because just as he is, so also are we in this world.
verse.note: ‘In this’ may point back to the mutual remaining of verse 16 or forward to the confidence and likeness described in the rest of the verse; the translation leaves both open. ‘He’ in ‘just as he is’ translates a pronoun (‘that one’) which this letter regularly uses for Jesus.

verse.text: There is no fear in love; rather, perfect love drives out fear, because fear has to do with punishment, and the one who fears has not been perfected in love.
We love because he first loved us.
verse.note: Many later manuscripts add an object, ‘him’ or ‘God’, and the King James Version follows them. The earliest witnesses have no object, which leaves the statement general. The verb form could also be read as an exhortation, ‘let us love’.

verse.text: If anyone says, “I love God,” and hates their brother or sister, that person is a liar; for whoever does not love their brother or sister, whom they have seen, cannot love God, whom they have not seen.
verse.note: The Greek word is the masculine ‘brother’, but in early Christian usage it regularly meant a fellow member of the community, man or woman. ‘Brother or sister’ conveys that range; several modern translations do the same. Some manuscripts make the last clause a question: ‘how can he love God, whom he has not seen?’

verse.text: And this command we have from him: that whoever loves God must also love their brother or sister.
Everyone who believes that Jesus is the Christ has been born of God, and everyone who loves the father loves also the one born of him.
By this we know that we love the children of God: when we love God and carry out his commandments.
For this is love for God: that we keep his commandments. And his commandments are not burdensome,
verse.note: The Greek is literally ‘the love of God’, which could mean either God’s love for us or our love for God. The definition that follows, keeping his commandments, shows that love directed toward God is meant here, and most modern translations agree.

verse.text: because everything born of God conquers the world. And this is the victory that has conquered the world: our faith.
And who is it that conquers the world, if not the one who believes that Jesus is the Son of God?

This is the one who came through water and blood, Jesus Christ: not with the water only, but with the water and with the blood. And the Spirit is the one who testifies, because the Spirit is the truth.
verse.note: The first readers evidently knew what this referred to; modern readers must infer it. The most widely held view is that the water is Jesus’ baptism and the blood his death, and that ‘not with the water only’ answers people who accepted the first but denied the significance of the second. Other proposals include the water and blood that flowed from Jesus’ side at the crucifixion (John 19:34), or baptism and the Lord’s Supper. The matter is disputed.

verse.text: For there are three that testify:

note.term: For there are three that testify:
note.traditional: For there are three that bear record in heaven, the Father, the Word, and the Holy Ghost: and these three are one. And there are three that bear witness in earth

verse.note: The King James Version has a longer text here naming the Father, the Word and the Holy Spirit as three witnesses in heaven. These words are absent from every early Greek manuscript and from the early translations. They appear in the Latin tradition and in only a handful of very late Greek manuscripts. Scholars are virtually unanimous that they are not original, and the SBLGNT omits them.

verse.text: the Spirit and the water and the blood, and the three are in agreement.
If we accept the testimony of people, the testimony of God is greater, for this is the testimony of God: that he has testified about his Son.
Whoever believes in the Son of God has the testimony within himself. Whoever does not believe God has made him a liar, because he has not believed in the testimony that God has borne about his Son.
And this is the testimony: that God gave us eternal life, and this life is in his Son.
verse.note: In Jewish usage of the period, ‘eternal life’ is the life of the age to come, so the phrase describes a kind of life as well as its unending length. In this letter that life is already possessed by those who have the Son. ‘Eternal’ is the standard rendering; a minority of translators prefer ‘life of the age to come’.

verse.text: Whoever has the Son has life; whoever does not have the Son of God does not have life.
I have written these things to you so that you may know that you have eternal life, you who believe in the name of the Son of God.
And this is the confidence we have before him: that if we ask for anything according to his will, he hears us.
And if we know that he hears us, whatever we ask, we know that we have the requests we have asked of him.

If anyone sees his brother committing a sin that does not lead to death, he shall ask, and he will give him life—to those whose sin does not lead to death. There is sin that leads to death; I do not say that he should make request about that.

note.term: a sin that does not lead to death

verse.note: The letter does not say what the ‘sin that leads to death’ is, and it remains uncertain. Leading proposals are the deliberate rejection of Christ by those who had left the community (2:19, 22), the Old Testament distinction between inadvertent and defiant sin, and sin punished by physical death. ‘Death’ most likely means spiritual death, the opposite of the ‘life’ the chapter has been describing.

The Greek does not say who gives life. Many translations supply ‘God’ as the subject. Grammatically the simplest reading is that the one who prays is the giver, in the sense that his prayer obtains life for the sinner. The translation leaves the pronoun as open as the Greek.

verse.text: All wrongdoing is sin, and there is sin that does not lead to death.
We know that everyone who has been born of God does not sin; rather, the one who was born of God keeps him safe, and the evil one does not touch him.
verse.note: The verb is in the present tense, and some translations render ‘does not keep on sinning’ to ease the tension with 1:8–10 and 5:16, which assume that believers do sin. Whether the tense alone can carry that weight is debated. Others take the statement as describing what is true of the believer in principle, or as an ideal stated absolutely.

note.term: the one who was born of God keeps him safe
note.traditional: he that is begotten of God keepeth himself

verse.note: The Greek shifts from ‘everyone who has been born of God’ (the believer) to a different verb form, ‘the one who was born of God’, which most scholars take to be Jesus, the Son, who protects the believer. Some manuscripts read ‘himself’ instead of ‘him’, giving the King James Version’s sense that the believer guards himself. The SBLGNT reads ‘him’.

verse.text: We know that we are from God, and the whole world lies in the power of the evil one.

note.term: lies in the power of the evil one

verse.note: The Greek is literally ‘lies in the evil’, and the form could be neuter (‘in evil’, as in the King James Version) or masculine (‘in the evil one’). Since verse 18 has just spoken of ‘the evil one’ as a person, nearly all modern translations take it as masculine. ‘To lie in’ someone is a Greek idiom for being dependent on them or under their control. The phrase is set against ‘we are in the true one’ in verse 20.

verse.text: And we know that the Son of God has come and has given us understanding, so that we may know the true one; and we are in the true one, in his Son Jesus Christ. This is the true God and eternal life.

note.term: This is the true God and eternal life
note.traditional: This is the true God, and eternal life

verse.note: ‘This’ may refer to Jesus Christ, the nearest name, which would make the sentence one of the New Testament’s most direct statements that Jesus is God. It may instead refer back to ‘the true one’, the Father, whom the verse has just distinguished from his Son. Scholars are divided, and the Greek does not settle it.

verse.text: Little children, guard yourselves from idols.
verse.note: The letter ends abruptly with a warning it has not prepared for. It may be meant literally, of the images of pagan worship that surrounded the readers. It may instead be figurative, of the false conceptions of God taught by the letter’s opponents, in contrast to ‘the true God’ just named. Both readings have scholarly support.
